questions.prompt:
Read the text:

"Two years ago, a new public library opened in our neighbourhood, but few teenagers came. Then a young volunteer started free coding clubs on Saturdays. News of the clubs spread quickly. Within months, the reading room was full of students, and many of them borrowed their first book there. Today, the library is the busiest place in town."

What is the writer's main message?

options.text: Libraries should only lend books, not teach coding.
Teenagers never read books in their free time.
A free activity made the library popular.
Saturday is the best day to open a library.

questions.explanation: Every sentence follows one story: an almost empty library became the busiest place in town after the free coding clubs started — that is the message of the whole text. The text praises the clubs, so it never says libraries should only lend books; "never read books" contradicts the students who borrowed their first book; and Saturday is one detail.

questions.prompt:
Read the text:

"Two years ago, a new public library opened in our neighbourhood, but few teenagers came. Then a young volunteer started free coding clubs on Saturdays. News of the clubs spread quickly. Within months, the reading room was full of students, and many of them borrowed their first book there. Today, the library is the busiest place in town."

What can we infer about the teenagers?

options.text: They borrowed many books before the clubs started.
The clubs, not the books, first brought them in.
They did not like the young volunteer at all.
They came to the library only to sleep.

questions.explanation: The clues: few teenagers came before the clubs, the room was full after them, and many students borrowed "their first book" there — so the clubs, not the books, first attracted them. That same "first book" contradicts the idea that they borrowed many books before, the success of the clubs contradicts a dislike of the volunteer, and sleeping has no clue at all.

questions.prompt:
Read the text:

"Two years ago, a new public library opened in our neighbourhood, but few teenagers came. Then a young volunteer started free coding clubs on Saturdays. News of the clubs spread quickly. Within months, the reading room was full of students, and many of them borrowed their first book there. Today, the library is the busiest place in town."

Language: join the two sentences with a relative pronoun.

"A young volunteer started coding clubs. The volunteer loves computers."
→ "A young volunteer ______ loves computers started coding clubs."

options.text: who
which
what
when

questions.explanation: The volunteer is a person, and the relative pronoun for people is "who" ("that" is also possible): "A young volunteer who loves computers…". "which" is for things, and "what" and "when" are question words that cannot replace a person.

questions.prompt:
Read the text:

"Two years ago, a new public library opened in our neighbourhood, but few teenagers came. Then a young volunteer started free coding clubs on Saturdays. News of the clubs spread quickly. Within months, the reading room was full of students, and many of them borrowed their first book there. Today, the library is the busiest place in town."

Language: complete the sentence.

"I visited the club last Saturday. At 10 o'clock, the students ______ a computer game together, and they finished it at noon."

options.text: have just created
created
was creating
were creating

questions.explanation: At 10 o'clock the game was still in progress — the students finished it only at noon — and an action in progress in the past takes the past progressive: were + verb-ing, "were creating", because "the students" is plural. "was" is for one person, "created" presents the game as already finished at 10, and the present perfect "have just created" cannot go with a finished time such as "last Saturday".

questions.prompt:
Read this paragraph a student wrote about the text:

"The library became popular for a clear reason. A young volunteer offered free coding clubs. These clubs attracted curious teenagers. My uncle bought a new car last week. As a result, a quiet building turned into a lively place."

Writing: which sentence breaks the unity of the paragraph and should be removed?

options.text: "A young volunteer offered free coding clubs."
"My uncle bought a new car last week."
"These clubs attracted curious teenagers."
"As a result, a quiet building turned into a lively place."

questions.explanation: Every sentence develops one idea — why the library became popular — except "My uncle bought a new car last week", which jumps to another topic and breaks the unity. The coding clubs and the curious teenagers are the reasons, and the sentence opening with "As a result" is the logical conclusion.

questions.prompt:
Read the text again, then look at these four sentences:

1. "But at first, few teenagers came."
2. "A new library opened in our neighbourhood."
3. "As a result, it soon became the busiest place in town."
4. "Then a young volunteer started free coding clubs."

Writing: what is the best order to form a well-organised paragraph?
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 is the general opening: the library opened. Sentence 1, with "But", contrasts with it (few teenagers came), sentence 4, with "Then", brings the change (the coding clubs), and sentence 3, with "As a result", comes after its cause and closes the paragraph: 2 – 1 – 4 – 3.
